analysis.one_liner: Removes federal criminal penalties for marijuana and funds record clearing and small-business entry.
analysis.headline: Chuck Schumer's bill to remove federal marijuana penalties was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee in May 2019 and never received a vote before the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would take marijuana off the federal list of banned drugs, wiping out federal criminal penalties for growing, selling, importing, and possessing it with intent to distribute. It would also give grants to states to erase or seal old marijuana-possession convictions, steer federal money to SBA loans for women- and minority-owned marijuana businesses, fund research on driving and health effects, and allow new limits on marijuana advertising to protect minors. It never left the Judiciary Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: People exposed to federal marijuana prosecutions and old records — disproportionately lower-income and minority communities — plus small and minority-owned businesses seeking to enter the legal marijuana market. Public defenders and legal aid providers would also gain dedicated funding, since half the expungement grants must go to them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Marijuana defendants, people with records, small entrepreneurs

how_it_helps.text: Removes marijuana and THC from the Controlled Substances Act schedules, eliminating federal criminal penalties for importing, exporting, manufacturing, distributing, and possessing marijuana with intent to distribute.

Authorizes $20 million a year for fiscal 2019-2023 in grants to states and localities to expunge or seal marijuana-possession convictions, with at least half going to public defenders or legal aid providers.

Creates a Marijuana Opportunity Trust Fund, funded with at least $10 million a year, for SBA loans to small businesses in the marijuana industry owned by women or socially and economically disadvantaged individuals.
Authorizes $50 million a year for federal research on detecting marijuana-impaired driving and $100 million a year for research on marijuana's health effects and medical uses, for fiscal 2019-2023.
Directs federal regulators to impose advertising and promotion restrictions on marijuana products if needed to protect people 18 and under.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers would fund roughly $170 million a year in authorized research and grant spending. The federal government would also give up its power to prosecute marijuana offenses, and the bill imposes no new federal tax or comprehensive regulatory regime on the newly legal market.

drawbacks.text: The bill removes criminal penalties without building a comprehensive federal regulatory or tax framework for the newly legal market, relying instead on annual Treasury estimates of existing tax revenue to fund its programs.
The bill itself acknowledges there is no reliable way to determine whether a driver is impaired by THC, which is why it authorizes $50 million a year to develop impairment-testing strategies.

A rule of construction preserves federal authority to stop marijuana trafficking from states that have legalized it into states that have not, so the interstate conflict with prohibition states would continue.
Advertising restrictions are left to regulator discretion and must stay within First Amendment limits, so youth-protection rules may be narrower than supporters would like.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — ending federal criminal penalties for conduct most states now permit or are moving to permit, and clearing old records — is large for ordinary people and disproportionately benefits communities hit hardest by enforcement. The costs are modest and mostly fiscal. The bill's main weakness is design, not cost: it legalizes without a full regulatory and tax structure, and it leaves open how to police impaired driving and interstate sales into prohibition states.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate introduced it and sent it to the Judiciary Committee, which never acted on it, and the bill died when that Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on May 20, 2019 by Sen. Chuck Schumer with eight Democratic cosponsors and one Independent.
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, and no further action was ever recorded.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2021 without the committee reporting the bill or either chamber holding a vote on it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Anyone who wanted federal marijuana prohibition to keep standing is better off, since the bill never reached a vote and federal criminal penalties remained on the books. Communities living under those penalties, and small and minority-owned businesses waiting for legal access to banking and federal loans, got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Keepers of the federal prohibition status quo

for.name: Chuck Schumer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to decriminalize marijuana and fund expungement and small-business assistance.

against.name: Lindsey Graham
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled a markup or advanced the bill out of committee.

against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held; the bill's nine cosponsors were all Democrats or allied independents, and no Republican signed on.

industries.note: Descheduling would lift the federal overhang on a legal-in-states industry and create federal small-business loan access for women- and minority-owned entrants. Its interest runs alongside the public's here, since the same change ends criminal exposure for growers, sellers, and consumers.

industries.industry: Federal and state drug law enforcement
industries.note: The bill eliminates federal marijuana trafficking offenses, removes marijuana from wiretap authorization, and strips marijuana-specific provisions from forest drug-control law, shrinking an enforcement mission and the funding that follows it.

industries.industry: Public defenders and legal aid providers
industries.note: At least half of the $20 million annual expungement grant pool is reserved to cover their costs, a direct funding stream for helping people clear old convictions.
The Marijuana Opportunity Trust Fund would channel at least $10 million a year into SBA 7(m) loans for women- and minority-owned marijuana businesses, a market lenders currently cannot touch.
